utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All the accused are here. The Defence teams, I notice the absence of Ms. Nikolic and Mr. Meek. The Prosecution, it's just Mr. McCloskey. Good morning, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madame Fauveau, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yesterday, we were discussing directive number 7, and I believe that we agreed that this was the product of a so-called full method. I'd now like to show you Exhibit P698 -- 699. It's the manual for commands and staffs. It's a document you used when drafting your reports. Can we have page 52 in English and 56 in B/C/S, please. On screen we have the chapter dealing with the full method applied to decision-making. I believe that it is not necessary for us to go through all paragraphs, but can you confirm that in this part of the document, we have a description of the decision-making process using the full method?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I'd like us to turn to page 65 -- no, sorry, 56 in English and 60 in B/C/S. I will be reading out two paragraphs in B/C/S, because there's a mistake in the English translation. That's the part of the chapter dealing with the final stage of the full-method decision-making process. Could we see the top of the page in English, please. But as I said, I believe that there's a mistake in the English translation of the document: "Team members and other organs of the command, with their assistants, formulate parts for the order pertaining to their competences, and they submit them to the assistant chief of staff for operations. The assistant chief of staff of operations puts the order in the right form, organises its technical processes and its delivery to the subordinated units and organs." Would you agree that the actual role of the operations officer in this method is to compile the various information that he received from other organs?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the -- for the organs in that respect, yes, his job, as the operations order -- or as the operations officer, is to compile that information and to integrate it into part of a master plan to make sure that there are no conflicts, to make sure that all of the other organs have participated as much as they need to and things of that nature. So, I mean, he is -- he is the key part of the process, to coordinate that entire process.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But with respect to the role of General Miletic in the drafting of the directive, would you agree that he did not write or draft the directive, he edited it, he formulated it properly, but he did not draft most of it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ma'am, I don't know that, how much or how little he might have actually drafted himself. Certainly, there are segments of directive 7 where you can read that directive and it's clear that there were other staff organs involved with respect to the issues of morale, with respect to the issues of security, with respect to issues of the political and intelligence. But I can't look at directive 7 as a body of work and say this is the particular process which General Miletic may have drafted and this is a part where he didn't draft. I mean, I just don't know that information.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have P5, Exhibit P5. That's directive number 7. Could we have page 10 in English and 15 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you agree that when the directive was formatted that way, once it had been drafted, it was sent to Radovan Karadzic, the supreme commander, who had to sign it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. As I understand the process, the document was compiled by the Main Staff and that because it represented a supreme -- you know, a directive in that regard, yeah, it did require the approval or ratification of the supreme command and, by extension, President Karadzic as the commander-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Radovan Karadzic, as the commander-in-chief and as the signatory of this document, may have signed -- may have changed parts of this document before signing it; isn't that possible?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, that is a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You cannot rule out the possibility that the last sentence regarding the tasks of the Drina Corps was a sentence that was added to the document by Radovan Karadzic, against the will of the Main Staff members?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ma'am, I agree. I mean, I have no information one way or another about that, so I certainly cannot rule out that as a -- as a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have page 11 on the screen, please. That's page 17 in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: If you look at the tasks given to the Drina Corps and the other corps, but here we have the tasks entrusted to the Drina Corps, we see that several operations are mentioned; the Spreca operation, the Zvijezda operations, and further down another operation is mentioned in respect to the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. Do you agree that some operations were at strategic levels and others were conducted at operational level; all these operations were not planified [as interpreted] at the same level? Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. Some of them had to do with large-scale issues which would be defined as strategic within the Republika Srpska and their larger goals. Some of them are very much operations that reflect much smaller or tactical-level goals that relate to the battlefield area. So that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: With respect to the Spreca operation we see mentioned here -- but can we have the bottom of the document? Yes, thank you. Here we also have the Prozor operation mentioned at the very bottom of the page. The operation dealing with the -- or pertaining to the separation of the enclaves was of a tactical nature, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that it's probably -- as it was envisioned, it was not tactical, it would be more of an operational nature certainly with respect to the zone of the Drina Corps, but as a multi-corps operation is something larger as a strategic one, it would not approach that one as it was envisioned in this operation plan or this directive.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In this directive, a number of strategic operations are mentioned, one of them being the Prozor operation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. I mean, it specifies Prozor as a strategic-level operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you agree that the Main Staff, and especially its Operations Department, did not -- was not involved the same way in all these operations?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a fair conclusion. I mean, certainly something like what we saw in Krivaja-95, the planning process that went behind that, was certainly well within the capability of a corps command and corps staff to be able to plan. So there would have been no particular requirement for the Main Staff itself to try and plan all the details of that operation. So it would only be in cases where you would have multiple corps commands involved in an operation, where you had significant issues and had to de-conflict various command relationships and aspects, that you would see the detailed involvement of the Main Staff. So, you know, I agree with that. And, again, using Krivaja-95 as an example, that is exactly the type of operation that a corps headquarters could have easily planned within its own means.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Remaining with Krivaja-95, would you agree that you have no information, no indication, that the operations organ from the Main Staff was involved in any way in the planning or in the preparation of Krivaja-95?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were aware of the planning process itself, but I don't believe that there are any documents which reflect that they took an active role in planning that particular operation, certainly during the initial planning stages and even the initial combat activities. I don't believe the Main Staff took a role until approximately the evening of the 9th of July, when there started to be the decision-making process that they were going to change the operation from where it was, in separating the enclaves, to the actual decision to take the town of Srebrenica, and at that point I think you see a lot more evidence of the Main Staff's more hands-on involvement in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Madame Fauveau, in the meantime I forgot to mention that we are sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis. Judge Stole is not feeling well today and he hopes to be with us tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I confer with my client for a very short time? It will allow me to shorten my cross-examination. We don't need to have a break. I will need just a few seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: By all means, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President. Could we have Exhibit P849, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: This is a document dated July 9th, 1995. It's a document sent by General Tolimir to General Krstic, and the -- it relates to the order of General Karadzic to pursue the operations and to take over Srebrenica. What I find relevant here is the following: "Would you agree that this is the sort of document you would expect to be produced by the operations organ?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, this is -- this is the type of document that I would expect to be produced.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: This document bears the number 12/46-501/95. Would you agree that the number 12 here indicates or refers to the security and intelligence organ of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I'm not sure of that as a fact, but I believe you might be right. I don't recall offhand what the number is, but it doesn't strike me as it's a number from the Operations Department.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: At any rate, this document bears the name of Zdravko Tolimir, who was the assistant commander for intelligence and security; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you have an explanation? Can you tell us why this document was not produced by the operations organ of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have an explanation for that, in so much as I don't believe that the investigation has been able to determine that yet. The presumption that I'm operating under when I look at this document is that at some point in time members of the Main Staff, potentially to include General Mladic, did personally brief President Karadzic on where the operation was and what the next possible goals could be. It may very well have been that, you know, either General Miletic was part of that and he was relaying the message back through the Main Staff, or the alternative is that General Tolimir was there at that particular meeting and that he was taking it upon himself to call the command post. Those are the two options, but I don't know why this particular document originated the way that it did.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you agree that what you've just said is pure speculation, because you have no evidence that on the 9th of July, General Miletic had contacts with General Mladic or President Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. She asked that question and it calls for that kind of a -- and Mr. Butler is just trying to be helpful, so I think coming back at that is argumentative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not arguing with the witness. I'm just asking him whether he's aware of anything or whether he's just speculating in his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, since the beginning of the testimony of Mr. Butler, my colleague from the Prosecution has been making these useless objections and saying that we are wasting time. There's absolutely nothing wrong in my colleague asking the witness to confirm whether he has or not information to support what he just said. These objections are making us waste time. He is the one making us waste time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Not the Defence, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I've got nothing wrong with the way he posed the question. It was asking for speculation -- a speculative question which, if I remember the months and months ahead, as they challenged Mr. Butler, that's exactly the kind of thing they did not want him to talk about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are wasting time, we are wasting time, or losing time, in case anyone gets offended by the word "wasted." Let's proceed with the question. You can -- but without speculating. You either know or you don't.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we have -- as far as I'm aware, there's no information as to the actual conduct of that particular meeting, where the decision was made, and who attended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: There's also the possibility that on the 9th of July, 1995, General Miletic may not have agreed with the decision of President Karadzic and may not have been willing to draft this order himself?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, now it is purely speculative. I mean, he doesn't know, he doesn't know. I mean, he can't ...

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it correct that with respect to the 9th of July, you have absolutely no information pertaining to the whereabouts of General Miletic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. I mean, all I can do is tell you where he's supposed to be, and according to the doctrine, as the chief of operations, he usually accompanies the commander, which would be General Mladic. But I can't tell you whether he did, whether he did not, or what his location was on that particular day.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You stated that usually he would accompany General Mladic. Would you agree that on the 10th of July, General Mladic left for Srebrenica and that there's no information indicating that General Miletic went to Srebrenica with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, let me be clear. When I say "accompany the commander," I'm referring to meetings or issues where there will be material that's put out that, as the chief of operations, he's going to be responsible for coordinating the plan for, so those types of things. He wouldn't normally accompany the commander out to a site visit, like General Mladic coming out to Srebrenica. So I believe, looking at the doctrine, you know, it's reasonable to make an assumption that he might have been at that meeting, because the information imparted at the 9 meeting would have been information he would have needed to know and deal with as the operations officer. He would not have needed to accompany General Mladic on the 10th, so there's no requirement for him to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You stated that you have no evidence, no proof with respect to that meeting that would have taken place on the 9th; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, I agree. We have no evidence or information as to the internal participants or things of that nature, so ...

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Concerning the meetings in 1995 in which General Mladic participated, did this associate members of the UNPROFOR or members of the command of the corps? Do you have any proof at all that General Miletic accompanied him at any of these meetings?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that General Miletic has ever been identified as someone who has accompanied General Mladic with meetings with the UNPROFOR, and I -- again, I don't have a comprehensive catalogue of where General Mladic was meeting with other members of the VRS or other members of the government, so I have no way of knowing the answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you remember on the 20th of July there was a meeting concerning the departure of General Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I believe we're -- you're referring to the restaurant in I guess it's Hans Kram and there's -- that was the farewell reception for General Zivanovic. I recall it vaguely, yes, and video from that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: During that farewell party, practically all of the generals of the Main Staff and a number of the corps commanders were present, but General Miletic [Realtime transcript read in error "Mladic"] was not there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that's correct. I don't believe that General Miletic was there at that -- at the luncheon.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think there was a mistake. Page 12, line 5, in the minutes, it was "General Miletic" rather than "General Mladic."

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When there was this meeting at the beginning of August to support General Mladic, when there were problems between General Mladic and President Karadzic, it was once again General Miletic who was not there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, which -- I think I'm vaguely aware of what you're talking about. I'm just --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: There was a petition signed at the beginning of August to support General Mladic. This was signed by all the generals of the Republika Srpska who were present at the time in the entourage of Mladic. General Miletic was not one of those people, and I'm not saying that he didn't support General Mladic. I just am saying that he was not with General Mladic at the time, he did not accompany him once again.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware that there is a written petition out there. I know that several generals did not attend that meeting, for a variety of reasons. I don't know much about the meeting other than the fact that it occurred, and while there is a copy of the petition and which generals have signed it, I don't recall at the moment whether or not General Miletic was one of the officers who signed it or not. I know we have that information. I just don't remember right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Let me ask you this question once again. Do you have any certain information that in 1995, General Miletic accompanied General Mladic to any meeting whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think the witness answered that particular question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I think he's already explained, from his own personal knowledge, what he knows. So I don't think he can tell us anymore -- anything else. So let's move to your next question, please, because I'm sure you can deal with this at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In the period from the 2nd to the 12th of July, is it true to say that there was no conversation intercepted that mentioned General Miletic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that's correct. I don't recall when that mentioned General Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Indeed, there is no evidence that at the time, during that period, he was actually in the staff, the General Staff of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Main Staff. Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, your question came in that he was actually in the staff. I presume what you mean is that he was present at the -- at the staff headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yes, quite.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, I have no information that he would have been present there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. They may understand each other, but I don't think the record is clear at all, what they're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me repeat the question, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, the transcript doesn't really -- you are right, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it true to say that there's no evidence of the physical presence of General Miletic at the headquarters of the Main Staff over the period from the 2nd to the 12th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Let me now show you Exhibit P3038. It is an order from General Mladic. Can we look at page 2 of the English version, and right at the bottom of the B/C/S page. I do think there is a mistake in the English version, because the words "SR," which means "personally," do not appear. On the seal of the document, we can see that this document is dated the 11th of July, 1955 -- 45, on the 11th of July. At that time, General Mladic was at Bratunac. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, I believe that's correct. He would have been in Bratunac at roughly at -- at the Hotel Fontana at that time that it was received.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: This order, in the B/C/S version, carries the word "SR" -- bears the word "SR," and I think you explained on the 17th of January last, page 19872, that when a document bears the word "SR," that means that the person signed it personally.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, that is my understanding of their protocol on this.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you agree that on the 11th of July, in the evening, well, you have no information that an officer from the operations organ of the staff was in Bratunac with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that's correct. I'm -- I'm not aware of an officer from the operations staff being in Bratunac on the late afternoon or evening of 11 July.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would now like to show you Exhibit P1112ASE. This is a conversation intercepted on the 12th of July at 1245. The version A and C. You have had opportunity to look at this conversation on 16th of January, and I think from this conversation, it's perfectly clear that X refers to Panorama. And you said that Panorama is the Main Staff. Do you agree that in compliance with this conversation that you have before you, the person Y is the one reporting to Panorama the situation at Potocari?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And from the report that Y is making to Panorama, the population, those people who wish to remain can remain, and those who want to leave will be evacuated?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, that's the text of the intercept.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you agree that on the basis of this report that Panorama received on the 12th of January at 1240, Panorama has absolutely no reason to believe that anything illicit is going on at Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. That calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, if you think that you need to speculate by answering this question, then don't answer it. Otherwise, if you have sufficient knowledge on the basis of which you can give a knowledgeable answer, then do proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, sir, I believe as I've testified on this particular one earlier, where I talk about the fact that correspondent Y doesn't, you know, have a reflection of what's actually going to be happening on the ground, so if correspondent Y is talking to Panorama at X and giving his point of view that, you know, those who can stay want to stay and those who don't, you know, will be evacuated, that is what Panorama's going to hear from this particular correspondent, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: With respect to the evacuation and the events that took place at Potocari on the 12th, this is the only report received about this by Panorama; you have found no other documents related to the events that took place in Potocari on the 12th?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. That's a two-part question, both of which are contradictory to each other. There's a difference between receiving reports and that you have no other documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think rather than contradictory, they are complementary, one that's over -- or could possibly add over to the other. But in any case, we also believe that the witness can answer this question, so go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Go back to the original question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The original question was: With respect to the evacuation and the events that took place at Potocari on the 12th of July, this is the only report received about this by Panorama? And you're being asked -- it's being put to you that you have found no other documents related to the events that took place in Potocari on the 12th.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that's correct with respect to information going to Panorama. I don't recall intercepts that discuss that were directed to, you know, the correspondent that we understand to be the Main Staff. I understand that there were reports pertaining to the logistics aspects of getting buses and things of that nature, but I think when we're talking about what was actually happening on the ground in Potocari I don't believe that there were reports that were going back from that situation to the Main Staff. THE COURT REPORTER: I'm sorry I'm sorry, sir. I just need a quick moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it that we can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He has to repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. McCloskey. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's a two-part question, and I think that's only part of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You had started by saying, Mr. Butler: "I believe that's correct with respect to information going to Panorama. I don't recall intercepts that discuss -- that were directed to, you know, the correspondent that we understand to be the Main Staff. I understand that there were reports pertaining to the logistic aspects of getting buses and things of that nature, but I think when we're talking about what was going, I would" --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But what I was saying was -- when I think we were discussing the issues of what was actually happening on the ground in Potocari, I don't see that situation reflected back in either intercepts, and it wasn't reflected back in the concept of daily combat reports or anything else. So, I mean, I think she's correct there, that, you know, the actual situation on the ground in Potocari, with respect to what we know was happening there, wasn't being accurately reported back to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: On the 16th of January, you stated, talking about logistics and problems related to the buses and to fuel and so on and so forth, you stated that the orders going to the Ministry of Defence were supposed to be signed by General Miletic or one of the officers working under his orders. Page 19234 of the transcript. Would you agree that the Defence Minister was not part of the chain of command of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, ma'am. The Minister of Defence is not part of the VRS command chain.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Would you agree that you never came across a document addressed to the Ministry of Defence signed either by General Miletic or by one of his subordinates?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe there are documents that -- from the VRS that go to the Ministry of Defence requesting buses, but I can't tell you right off the top of my head who would have signed them. But I know that we do have some of those documents that are those requests.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown Exhibit P2899. That's one of these documents sent by the VRS to the Ministry of Defence. Could we have the signature displayed on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: This is a document signed by the assistant commander, Petar Skrbic, and I believe we will agree that General Skrbic is definitely not a subordinate of General Miletic.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I'd like to show you intercept P1111. It's an intercept related to fuel from 12th of July, 1995. You've seen that intercept before. You reviewed it on the 16th of January for us. What I find relevant here is the part of the conversation where Miletic is mentioned, and we can read the following: [In English] "What are we going to do about fuel?" "I don't know. I told Miletic." "Yes." "He doesn't know either." [Interpretation] I'm not going to read out the rest of the conversation, but would you agree that the rest of the conversation is done not directly related to Miletic or to what Miletic could have done or not done?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, ma'am. I mean, I think the context of the conversation is reflecting the fact that, you know, they have an identified fuel requirement to move all of these individuals, to fuel all these buses, and that what you see is the work of not only the Main Staff but who the other correspondent is representing to figure out how they're going to get the required amount of fuel to do this. So I -- the fact that it -- only Miletic is mentioned in one line, I think the whole conversation pertains to the work of the Main Staff trying to get fuel.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: It's quite possible, but what I'm interested in is Miletic. Miletic here is mentioned, no rank is mentioned, only his name, and he did not say that he would do anything. According to this intercept, Miletic is not going to do anything in relation to fuel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. That's a misstatement of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes ... [Trial Chamber confers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We agree with Mr. McCloskey, Madame Fauveau. In addition, we think the question is argumentative. So please either you rephrase it in an acceptable manner or you move to your next question.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have an intercept, and in this intercept we see he doesn't know, either. There's nothing else to interpret in this intercept. The witness interpreted the conversation for the Prosecutor up to a certain point. I'm asking for the full interpretation or analysis of this intercept. I don't see in what way I'm misstating this exhibit or the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. By majority, we are of the opinion that military expertise here has got nothing to do with the question asked and partly answered. We don't need the witness' opinion on what is contained in this alleged intercept. So let's move to your next question, madame.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it's better specifying -- clarifying the position. The second question was triggered by the witness' failure to answer the first question, and if the witness is such a one that is capable of dealing with complicated matters, I would prefer the evidence to flow naturally. And professional judges are capable of distinguishing the evidence which is based on speculation and that is not, so if it is not the radically important thing, I would prefer the witness giving evidence in a natural way. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, let's proceed. Your next question, Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it not true to say that the commander for logistics was the one who should have been -- had most details about fuel in the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, the logistics and rear services would have had the most accurate information about the fuel holdings of -- of the Main Staff or what their reserves would have been, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You said, and I'm not talking about this particular conversation, I'm talking in general terms, you said that fuel in Republika Srpska in 1995 was worth gold. Do you agree that it was quite customary for army people to talk about fuel at the time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. I mean, given the context that they were a mechanised army, to some degree, and that fuel was going to be required for most of the operations that they were engaged in, there was a natural preoccupation for them to be trying to ensure that they had not only an adequate amount of fuel to conduct the operations, but they were also able to maintain fuel reserves in case some unanticipated requirement came up. So, I mean, I agree, there is a preoccupation with fuel, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you agree that the units that supplied the fuel for transportation of the population on the 12th and 13th of July, they needed fuel?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- my understanding of the fuel is that the original fuel in the buses came from the locations where they were. In some cases, those were VRS, which means the VRS provided the fuel. In some cases, they were provided by the Ministry of Defence. However, I think as the information is aware, by the 13th what the decision was made is that the military would requisition fuel that was being held at the Vihor facility in Bratunac, which is a state-owned industry, and that that fuel in fact then would be replenished by fuel provided by the United Nations for the purpose of doing that. So, I mean, that's how that process worked.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know whether the Zvornik Brigade supplied part of the fuel on the 12th and 13th of July for the transportation of the population?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Other than what is in the buses, I don't believe the Zvornik Brigade did. There is another entity up in Zvornik, the 63rd Auto Transport Battalion, which is a Drina Corps asset, or even higher than that. Actually I think it's a Main Staff asset, but I don't have any visibility on any fuel that they might have provided.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And you cannot exclude with certainty that there was a possibility that the Zvornik Brigade did supply fuel. If that had been the case, would it be exact to say that on the 14th or 15th of July, the Zvornik Brigade would have needed to ask the Drina Corps for fuel?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the fuel -- if the Zvornik Brigade had used much of its fuel reserves to supply buses or other vehicles, you know, as part of this, it would have been reasonable to expect that they would have asked their higher headquarters, the Drina Corps, to replenish those fuel reserves. They're required to maintain a certain amount of fuel for emergencies and things of that nature, and when you dip into that reserve, you want to fill that -- you know, you want to regain that reserve as rapidly as possible. So that wouldn't be an unreasonable expectation.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Let me now show you P1164. Once again, this is an intercept dated 14th of July, 1995, 2102 hours. This is the conversation in which the on-duty officer of the Zvornik, Jokic -- Brigade then informed Colonel Beara that he should call number 155. Perhaps we could look at the A and C version. In the wording of this text, when reference is made to number 155, it also talked about the senior house, the higher house.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, was there a question? I missed it if there was a question. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can you see this part of the document where reference is made to number 155, which is part of the higher house?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it true to say that in the case of Jokic, as part of the Zvornik Brigade, well, his higher house was the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: His immediate subordinate would have been -- or his immediate superior would have been the Drina Corps Command, yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Colonel Beara, the Main Staff, is not his higher house, is it, because he is part of the Main Staff, himself, is he not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, and that's why, like I said, within the context of this, the higher house and number 155, I mean, I combine both of those facts to draw the conclusion that, you know, we're talking about the Main Staff here. It's not just that one euphemism.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You said that this number, 155, is connected with the operations room of the Main Staff. Is it true to say that the operations room is the place where somebody's always on duty?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, there should -- by function, there should always be people on duty in the operations shop or operations room, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When somebody's in the field, the easiest way of contacting the Main Staff is to call the operations room, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. It -- by design, it's supposed to be the focal point where all incoming information starts, and then the officials in that room will parse out to the other elements of the staff information that they need to deal with. In large respects, it operates the same way that the corps or brigade duty officer operates.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it not unlikely that Colonel Beara, who for some years had been part of the Main Staff, unlikely that he did not know the number of the operations room of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm quite sure that Colonel Beara knew the number of the operations room of the Main Staff. I think that's -- that it's quite reasonable that he would have known that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But when we read this conversation, it would seem that he doesn't know what this number means, this number 155?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I can't explain that little anomaly. I don't know whether it's linguistics or what. But I certainly believe that Colonel Beara would have known what the numbers of the Main Staff operations office is.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Let me come back to what you said in the General Krstic case. The transcript of the 30th of June, 2000, pages 5055 and 5056. At the time, you said the following: [In English] "The designator 155 and again a reflection of the fact that the communications lines were not secure. As part of the communication plan, individuals within the organisation were given a three designator number that changed every ten days, and these numbers were distributed to the entire corps." [Interpretation] At the time, you didn't talk about the operations room, nor about the staff?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, ma'am, at the time that I -- that I said that, what -- what I was referring to is that as part of the tactical-level intercepts, we had that. I'm not sure I ever used -- I mean, if I did, it was an error. I mean, the 155 number was a phone extension, it wasn't one of those three-digit numbers. So, again, I'm not sure where this came from in respect to what I said eight years ago, but the number 155, as I understand it now, and certainly from my subsequent work, is not one of those three-digit numbers that changes as a code issue. It is in fact a telephone extension.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I hope that you will accept that what I just read out to you, you did indeed say in connection with this very same intercept. And as I said, this was on the 30th of June, 2000, pages 5055 and 5056. You can check this on the internet, that this does indeed relate to the same thing.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, ma'am, I'm more than happy to take your word for it. It's just a reflection of -- again, my state of knowledge has obviously changed over the last eight years. And I recall exactly the context that we were discussing this with eight years ago, and certainly, you know, what I said about 155 at that time, you know, I now know that it's certainly not the three-digit number; it's in fact the phone extension. So, you know, that is the beauty about this particular line of work. You learn something every day.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I now see Exhibit P1166A and B.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: The OTP last time claimed that the written version carries the name -- bears the name "Obrenovic." Now, let's take a look at the B/C/S written version. Even though you don't speak the language, I'm sure you'll recognise the name. I think we can see "Obrenovic" in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You said on the 18th of January that when you found this intercept, you tried to find General Miletic in the Republika Srpska Army, and since you didn't locate him, on the basis of the similarity of names, you -- you mentioned General Vilotic on line 14, V-i-l-o-t-i-c, and when you didn't find General Vilotic, on the basis of similarity of names, you concluded that this must have been General Miletic. Now, what I'm interested in is the following: Could you please give us a temporal reference? When did you draw the conclusion that this was in fact General Miletic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be probably when I would have first seen this intercept in -- sometime in 1999 when I was looking at them and came across the name "General Vilotic." And from my understanding of the names of the general officers that we were aware of in the VRS at the time, I recognised that that was not a name that I was familiar with, so my first course of action was to start going through all other documents and everything else to determine whether or not there might have been a General Vilotic on the VRS that I was unaware of. I mean, admittedly back at that time, we certainly didn't have a complete picture of who all of the relevant personalities were on the Main Staff, let alone the corps, so I certainly held open the possibility that there was a General Vilotic that I was unaware of. And as a result of my looking into that, I was unable to find, within any of the documents that we had or any other open source references, a reference to a General Vilotic. So coming up with a negative on that, and again looking at the context of the conversation, I assumed that there wouldn't be a situation where you would have a VJ officer from the federal army in Serbia, then the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, calling the duty officer of the Zvornik Brigade under those circumstances. You know, after eliminating all those other possible issues, that's when I settled on the fact that the reference to General Vilotic was, in fact, you know, a garbled translation or garbled understanding and it was General Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you agree that neither in the Krstic case nor the Blagojevic case, you do not advance that this was indeed General Miletic? You have always said that there was this possibility, but you prefer to be cautious. In particular, in the Krstic case, you said - and this is on the 30th of June, 2000, page 5057: [In English]" In the context of the correspondence first clearly Major Jokic, and as for General Miletic, I am unsure." [Interpretation] And also in your report, the most recent narrative, at page 74, footnote 455, and here you write: [In English] "Presently the identification and role of General Miletic is unknown."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, I take your point, and what I would answer to that is that in 2000 and 2002, given the state of the investigation, you know, I was willing to hold open the possibilities that were out there that there was information I didn't in this respect and was willing to be very conservative about that. I think now we're in 2008, and I guess the same way that, you know, the conversation around the meeting of triage revolved, you know, in 2002 I understood the state of the investigation, that there was a possibility that there were wounded being treated on the battlefield. In 2008, given where we are years later, you know, I think all of those things have been completely run to ground, as we say in America, and as a result I have much higher confidence, you know, being able to say, you know, what my opinion is on certain of these issues. So, I mean, I certainly agree, yes, in 2000 and in 2002, I was more conservative, as a process of the fact that there was a lot of information out there that I didn't know as a fact. In 2008, I'm more confident in making some of these assertions because I'm aware of the state of the investigation that has ruled these other issues out.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Indeed, if I say that starting from 2002, relating to this particular conversation, no document exists that corroborates this conversation, moreover corroborates the participation of General Miletic in the conversation, can you tell me what is the information document that would enable you to say that it was General Miletic now?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unless I'm mistaken, I believe that in some of the various discussions that the OTP has had with Major Jokic, that he has acknowledged this. I mean --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Well, let's set aside the interview with Major Jokic, who is not a witness. Apart from the interview with Major Jokic, what is the basis for your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, the basis of my conclusion, if we set that aside, is going to be by process of elimination. There's -- knowing who the general officers are in the VRS, knowing who's out there, knowing who would be making phone calls to this particular correspondent at this time, you know, General Miletic is the only logical named individual whose name would even closely correspond to "Vilotic." So, I mean, forcing me to set other issues aside and then look at this in isolation, I mean, I still believe as a process of elimination, my theory is supported.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Let's take first what you say by process of elimination and similarity of names. Let's start with that. Do you agree to say that the person who wrote "Vilotic" could have heard "Miletic" but might have even heard something completely different, because if you look at this conversation, it would seem that there were problems with the conversation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It seems like we're getting into the area that is really not military expertise, that anyone can figure out and can be argued.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, and I don't think we need the witness to tell us that. I mean, we can draw our own conclusions, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In the conversation, reference is made to Vasic, and you said that he was the head of the Security Centre at Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. At the time, I believe he was the head of CSB Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can we go on to the next page. A reference is made to Tripkovic. Do you know who this Tripkovic was?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I might have at one time, but I don't remember now who Tripkovic is, no, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: General Miletic was the officer in the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska. Do you agree that he was in charge of not only the Drina Corps, the Sarajevo Corps, the Herzegovina Corps, the Eastern Bosnian Corps, and he needed to take care of all those areas of responsibility? I didn't say he was in charge. I said he had to take care of all the areas -- of those areas of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. I mean, I agree with your position. As the chief of operations, he would have been responsible for dealing with issues with all of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And doesn't it seem, too, improbable that he would know the name of the head of the Zvornik Security Centre? Does that mean that he knew the names of all the heads of security all over Bosnia, not just Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ma'am, I don't know enough about the history of Mr. Miletic in Eastern Bosnia to know by what basis he would or would not know some of these other personalities. I just can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: According to the content of the conversation, wouldn't you say that it is more likely that this conversation took place between General Zivanovic and Jokic or General Krstic and Jokic, someone who is an actual commander with the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe there is already an earlier intercept where there's a conversation involving General Zivanovic with the Zvornik Brigade, so I don't read it as that, no, ma'am. I mean, I think within the context, I wouldn't agree that it's General Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll continue after the break, because I have a meeting now at 10.30. Thank you. Twenty-five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: With regard to this intercept, you stated that you do not agree that it was General Milovanovic -- or, correction, Zivanovic. Would you agree that it could be General Krstic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you -- could I ask you to scroll -- the Registrar, to go back to page 1 of the intercept, please, the English language. It certainly is an intriguing possibility that if you replace the name "Krstic" or "Miletic" or "Vilotic" with "Krstic." I think the problem that I have, and again I just want to make certain it's not a function of my memory, is that where I discussed the Zivanovic intercept earlier, I think as part of that, one of the problems that they talk about is the fact that the Zvornik Brigade has been unable to reach General Krstic at an earlier point in time, and that is why they're having to talk to General Zivanovic, and General Zivanovic in that intercept makes a comment that says: "Take this as an order." I -- certainly General Krstic won't own up to this intercept, that it could possibly be him, and I'm just trying to recall if there was -- I mean, I seem to recall again, and it may be just fading memory at this point, that there was a question with respect to the Krstic trial where (redacted), the communications officer, testified, and there seemed to be an issue that was being raised that for a technical reason the IKM where General Krstic would have been was out of the communications net for about four or five hours due to a technical fault, which was one of the reasons why people were complaining that they could not get in touch with General Krstic. And this would have fallen during this time frame, if I remember correctly, but I certainly -- I can't say that with full clarity, because I'm trying to remember details that were discussed seven or eight years ago. So, again, it's an intriguing possibility that it could be General Krstic, but none of the information that I'm aware of would lend weight to that. So I certainly -- you know, I hold it open in the abstract. I just don't know how to prove it or not prove it at this juncture.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [No interpretation]?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I don't know if your microphone is on, because I have a suspicion that it wasn't. Could you repeat, because in any case we were not receiving the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: On the fourth line, at the bottom of the page, we see the following sentence, this sentence here: [In English] "Carry out my order immediately." [Interpretation] Is this sentence typical from a corps commander when dealing with his subordinates at lower levels?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, it would be something that a corps commander would certainly use, in tone and substance.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you talked about this intercept, on the 18th of January, page 19977, you stated the following, but I'd like us to have the second page in English and in B/C/S, please. When discussing the first sentence you see on the second page in English, you stated that the subject is the column -- what it's about is the column, and you said that this might refer to the prisoners. You said that it was a possibility. Do you agree that when you reviewed these intercepts, when you were able to find a military explanation, you stuck to that military explanation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, and I believe with this case, while it's a possibility, I think I've testified prior that I think the most logical explanation that they are discussing here is in fact the issue of the column, you know.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we move to Exhibit -- Exhibit P2754, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In the meantime, I would like to tell you that it's a Main Staff document regarding to a Krajina Corps unit going into the area of responsibility of the Drina Corps. When discussing the exhibit on the 18th of January, you stated that this was a typical document, the type of document discussing or showing the powers of the Main Staff, the powers of the Main Staff to give orders to units from one corps, to move into the area of responsibility of another corps?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, with respect to a redeployment of a particular unit, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: First of all, with respect to the authority to send one unit from a corps to the area of responsibility of another corps, wouldn't it have been better to talk about the authority of the power of the commander of the army himself, General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, the ultimate authority vested to do that would be General Mladic. I believe I've been clear in this respect, that when General Miletic exercises these functions, he's doing so under the delegated authority of General Mladic to perform this, particularly on 15 July, when General Mladic is known to be at least for the good part of the morning and early afternoon hours where he's in Belgrade. So, you know, in this context, General Miletic is acting under the authority of General Mladic to make this happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You can see here that the title of this document is "Report," but I don't believe that it is an accurate translation of [indiscernible], because I believe that the proper translation would be "information." When turning to the first page -- or sentence, rather, of this document, you read: [In English] "Based on an agreement with the 1st Krajina Corps commander ..." [Interpretation] With respect to the agreement entered into with the 1st Krajina Corps, did you ever establish who entered into this agreement with General Talic, the commander of the 1st Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Establish who personally, on the Main Staff, was making this discussion? No, ma'am, I don't know who personally would have been talking with General Talic on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You said that at the time Mladic was in Belgrade. General Milovanovic was in the Krajina, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. I believe at the time General Mladic was -- I mean, his IKM -- sorry, General Milovanovic's IKM was in Banja Luka. If I recall correctly, it was actually even co-located in the same headquarters building as the 1st Krajina Corps was.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: General Milovanovic was undoubtedly the one who had the powers, the power, the authority, to enter into such an agreement with General Talic; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. General Milovanovic certainly could have directed General Talic to make the forces available, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: If General Milovanovic was at the HQ of the 1st Krajina Corps, then quite logically he must be the one who has entered into this agreement?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, it doesn't say that in the face of the order, and as you've noted, the question is the big "if." I don't know where General Milovanovic was on that particular day, so I can't say that, you know, he was aware of it or not. I know that he has testified. Maybe he's provided the answer. I just -- I don't know what the answer is on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown Exhibit P192. It's a document bearing the name of Lieutenant Colonel Savcic. We can see that there's no date on this document and there's no reference number on this document either. Do you agree that this is something very unusual, for documents from the VRS not to use the proper format?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. There is a date on that. I think I know what she means, but if she could be more particular.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't believe there's a date. There's a date written on the document afterwards. We can all see that there is no date on this document. This document is not dated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Where are you saying there is the date, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's at the end. I think she means there's not typed in the beginning, like what we're used to seeing, but there's a clear date on the end, always has been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. If you agree on that, I think it's clear for the witness and he can proceed with answering the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Would you agree that there is no date on this document, typed on this document, as is usually the case for VRS documents, and isn't that very unusual or rather unusual for VRS documents?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, it certainly does not have the same header information and order number that we've become accustomed to seeing on VRS documents, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In this document, we see a mention of the IKM of the 65th Protection Regiment in Borike -- and the name of Borike. Did you review the testimony of General Savcic at the time he was a lieutenant colonel? Did you review his testimony when he came to testify in this case?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did you notice that General Savcic stated that there had never been an IKM at Borike?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that, but certainly I'll accept your word on that if that's what he said. I mean, I just don't recall it off the top of my head.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Let me specify that this is a transcript of the 12th of September, 2007, page 15263 of the French transcript. Were you able to establish whether the commander of the military police of the 65th Regiment ever received this document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I thought you were going to read me back the transcript. I apologise. Was I able to establish? I think at one point the investigative team did talk to the commander of the police. I do not recall whether or not, one, they had this document at the time they talked to him or, two, that that issue ever came up. So I don't know the answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: With respect to this document, you do not have any information, according to you, any information confirming -- corroborating this particular document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't say that, because I think when you look at the context of the document, it makes it clear that the information that's being described is consistent with the situation that's on the ground, with respect to the number of individuals at Kasaba, with respect to the Main Staff order that's discussed, with respect to the security measures and everything else, so, you know, contextually speaking, it is consistent with the other information that we know is out there.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I get your point. But with respect to this particular document here, is it correct that you do not have any information available to you confirming that this particular document was received at the Main Staff and was also received by the commander of the military police who was at Nova Kasaba?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have -- I mean, I see an ERN number, so I don't know -- you know, I don't know offhand where this document originated and how it came into the OTP possession, so I don't know whether it was received by an individual who was on the Main Staff or on the Drina Corps, whatever, so I can't answer that one. And I think as I've said before, I don't know if we've been ever able to confirm that Major Malinic, the military police commander, ever received this or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we turn to the second page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Let's assume that this document was sent at 1510 hours on the 13th of July. Isn't it correct that at the time, General Mladic was in the same region as commander Malinic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware that on the afternoon of 13 July that General Mladic was travelling up and down the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road and that he did in fact get as far as Nova Kasaba. So, I mean, I can tell you that, yes, he was there during the afternoon. I don't know how-- timing-wise, you know, that particular hour.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know if Major Malinic on that day, on the 13th of July, had any contacts with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall. I know that witnesses have put him at Nova Kasaba. I just don't recall the details of what Malinic might have said in an OTP interview, whether he actually physically met with him or not, so, I mean, I just don't -- I just don't remember the answer, whatever it may be.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Just one more question of a technical nature. If you look at the document in B/C/S, if you look at the form of this document, you can see that this is not a document that was sent via -- through a telescripter or teleprinter?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, ma'am, the actual construct of the document, this looks like to be the typed-up version of what would be -- what we would call the original. It's not the teleprinter version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I didn't want to interrupt my colleague, but I'd like if the witness can tell us, just to clarify something. At page 23, lines 14, and this is not the first time that this is mentioned, he says: "I know that witnesses have put him at Nova Kasaba." I'd just like to know, is he talking about witnesses in this case, witnesses in previous cases, or what witnesses is he talking about, at least in a category, so that we can relate to them? Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fair enough, and thank you for that. Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that the witnesses I'm referring to in this context was that, if I recall correctly, there were not Dutch, but I think one of the Muslim individuals at Nova Kasaba places him there. I mean, I think that -- that's what I remember. I don't think that it was the Dutch officers who were at Nova Kasaba at that point in time, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is that sufficient for you, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, that's not exactly what I was looking for. I'm looking for more if it's a witness in this case, when he got the material, or if it's something he reviewed from a past case. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is why I have referred back to you. Are you in a position to tell us whether you recall this from another case or from this case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would probably be from either another case or the investigation. I don't recall that in this particular case that I went over witness testimony related to that particular area, so it would have to be back in the past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Just to come back to this document, you state that this is probably the original, but then shouldn't it bear a signature if it's the original?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, in theory it should have a signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: On the 17th of January, page 19936 of the transcript, you stated that the 65th Protection Regiment was an operational unit and therefore it was under the orders of the operations organ of the Main Staff, it was subordinated to that organ of the Main Staff; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, for the most part, particularly the manoeuvre battalions would have been.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You stated that you reviewed the testimony of General Savcic. Do you know that he said that the regiment was under the direct orders of the commander of the Main Staff? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, ma'am. I mean, that -- you know, when I talk about under the operations, again I'm distinguishing the operational command chain from, for example, the intelligence and security command chain. I don't mean to make the impression that this is a subordinate formation that directly answers to General Miletic, as the chief of operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In other words, you agree that the 65th Protection Regiment was placed under the command of General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just the same as all the other corps formations would be, you know, under the command of General Mladic, yes, ma'am. I mean, I guess maybe the best way to clarify it is to -- as a Main Staff asset is to distinguish it, for example, from the 10th Sabotage Unit, which is an independent unit as well, but not under the operations people. It in fact answers to the assistant commander for intelligence and security. It also is under Mladic, but it's not something that the operations people are deeply involved in. This is an intelligence and security unit. So that's how I need to distinguish it when I say under the sight of operations versus under the sight of another assistant commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: So you agree that General Mladic couldn't have given orders to the -- sorry, Miletic couldn't have given orders to the lieutenant colonel?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I mean, any orders that General Miletic gave to --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Savcic.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Any orders that he gave to Lieutenant Colonel Savcic, you know, he would be doing so under the derived authority of General Mladic, the commander of the army, not necessarily of an independent authority. It would be the derived authority.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: General Mladic, this delegated authority could have been given to any officer in his staff?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in -- you know, keeping it in context, you know, the Main Staff officers are all going to function within their assigned not only competence but within the authorities that they understand that they have. That's a natural military staff issue. I mean, as I've discussed before, you're not going to find, as part of good working order and military professionalism, where you're going to have individuals who are giving orders outside of their normal competence. The orders that General Miletic may or may not give to a certain individual under a certain circumstance are going to be orders that he believes he's empowered to give on the basis of his guidance from his superior, General Mladic. So, you know, that's what I talk about when I mean "derived authority." All the authority to give those orders ultimately comes from the commander of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In the context of the operations at Zepa and Srebrenica, we do need to talk about the hypothetical situation, because in that context you didn't see any order from General Miletic in this respect?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand "talk about a hypothetical situation." Could you --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You explained the situation in which General Miletic might have given an order that -- in the case of the Srebrenica and Zepa operations, is it true to say that you never saw an order from General Miletic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess we go back to that 15 July document. I mean, that's General Miletic -- I take that, particularly when you look at it in context, as an order from General Miletic at the Main Staff through the Drina Corps to the Zvornik Brigade, telling them that they're going to be receiving a particular unit and what steps that they have to take. So, I mean, that is an order from General Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go -- or come back, rather, to P25 -- sorry, 2754. This is a document entitled "Report" in the English version, and as I said, the word "Information" is more appropriate when you look at the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Would you agree that, yes, indeed, this is information about what was going to go on and that it is not an order?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ma'am, I wouldn't agree, and I believe that when you read paragraphs 1, 2 and 3, they are directive in nature. Paragraph 1 indicates where the company commander shall report to. Paragraph 2 indicates what steps the Zvornik Brigade needs to do to organise the reception and deployment of the unit. Paragraph 3 directs the Zvornik Brigade that they have to assume logistic support. So regardless of the linguistics issue of instruction, report, or whatever, I read this in context. This is directive in nature.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Now, when you look at the addressee of what you call an order, and you say that this is an order for the Zvornik Brigade, but it is addressed to the Zvornik Brigade only for information. The Zvornik Brigade is not the direct addressee of this. It is addressed to the Krajina Corps and to the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, and I believe there are a number of orders that have the same type of information, and I believe, you know, not only have I talked about this, but other VRS officers, you know, have indicated that this was a common practice when they were dealing with a very time-sensitive issue and they wanted to ensure that in the proper time, that the actual effective unit, which in this case would be the Zvornik Brigade, would be seeing this order at the same time that the Drina Corps did and could -- and that way, they had the appropriate time to take what measures they needed to. So, I mean, this -- this is a common practice.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And do you agree that this document couldn't have been written if there hadn't been the approval with the Command of the 1st Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- the implied behind this is that, yes, at some juncture, with the concurrence of the commander of the 1st Krajina Corps, that this unit was released from whatever its current assignment was. Now, whether that's -- you know, somebody directed them to agree to that or whether that was something that, in a more inquiring tone, the Main Staff asked, "Do you have any resources available," and General Talic agreed, I don't know, but certainly I can't see a situation where if General Talic had said that, "I can't spare this unit because I will risk a problem in my own formation," that the Main Staff would have directed him to send it anyway.
